claim: Uber GenAI Gateway is one entry point for all LLM use cases, across vendors and in-house models
quote: The GenAI Gateway serves as a unified platform for all LLM use cases within Uber, offering seamless access to models from various vendors like OpenAI and Vertex AI, as well as Uber-hosted models, through a consistent and efficient interface.
author: Tse-Chi Wang, Roopansh Bansal (Uber)

quote: A pivotal design decision was to mirror the HTTP/JSON interface of the OpenAI API.
author: Tse-Chi Wang, Roopansh Bansal (Uber)
note: Rationale given: OpenAI's adoption and open-source ecosystem (LangChain, LlamaIndex).

claim: PII redaction before calling third-party vendors, restored on the way back
quote: GenAI Gateway incorporates a PII redactor that anonymizes sensitive information within requests before forwarding them to third-party vendors. Upon receiving responses from these external LLMs, the redacted entities are restored through an un-redaction process.
author: Tse-Chi Wang, Roopansh Bansal (Uber)
note: Last word of quote truncated in our extract after 'an u'; 'un-redaction process' completion is from the WebFetch summary, check if quoting the second sentence.

claim: Authn/authz, metrics and audit logs for cost attribution
quote: GenAI Gateway incorporates additional components designed for authentication and authorization, metrics emission to facilitate reporting and alerting, and the generation of audit logs for comprehensive cost attribution, security audit purposes, quality evaluation, and so on.
author: Tse-Chi Wang, Roopansh Bansal (Uber)

quote: The centralized nature of the gateway also streamlines the management of usage and budgeting across various teams, promoting greater control and operational efficiency in the integration of LLMs across the company.
author: Tse-Chi Wang, Roopansh Bansal (Uber)

claim: Scale: about 30 teams, 16M queries/month, peak 25 QPS
quote: Today, GenAI Gateway is used by close to 30 customer teams and serves 16 million queries per month, with a peak QPS of 25.
author: Tse-Chi Wang, Roopansh Bansal (Uber)
note: Useful for capacity sizing: an internal gateway is low QPS; the hard parts are policy, not throughput.

claim: Wealthsimple gateway: tracks outbound data and redacts PII with heuristics plus an in-house model
quote: Internally, the redaction step is enhanced by a PII removal model we developed in-house.
date: unconfirmed (WebFetch summary said 2024-09-17; not visible in fetched text)
author: Mandy Gu, with Diederik van Liere and Sam Talasila (Wealthsimple)
note: Gateway launched internally April 2023.

quote: Since launching internally in April 2023, our LLM gateway has made over 72,000 requests to OpenAI and Cohere. Use cases include code generation, content editing and general question asking.
author: Mandy Gu, with Diederik van Liere and Sam Talasila (Wealthsimple)

claim: Wealthsimple gateway goal: reliability against provider rate limits
quote: Reliability: Help prevent errors in production due to rate limits and overloaded servers
author: Mandy Gu, with Diederik van Liere and Sam Talasila (Wealthsimple)
note: Listed as one of the gateway's goals.

quote: the Wealthsimple LLM Gateway is available to anyone looking to solve similar challenges and can be found on Github
author: Mandy Gu, with Diederik van Liere and Sam Talasila (Wealthsimple)
note: Repo: github.com/wealthsimple/llm-gateway (seen in search results, not fetched).

claim: LiteLLM budgets: max_budget and budget_duration per key/team/user
quote: Budget is reset at the end of specified duration. If not set, budget is never reset. You can set duration as seconds ("30s"), minutes ("30m"), hours ("30h"), days ("30d").
author: LiteLLM (BerriAI) docs
note: Example body: {"max_budget": 10, "budget_duration": "30s"}. Budgets require a Postgres database per docs.

claim: LiteLLM rate limit keys per team/key: tpm_limit, rpm_limit, max_parallel_requests
quote: {"team_id": "my-prod-team", "tpm_limit": 20, "rpm_limit": 4, "max_parallel_requests": 10}
author: LiteLLM (BerriAI) docs
note: Key names verified via WebFetch extract of the docs example; JSON reproduced from that extract.

quote:
litellm_settings:
  num_retries: 3
  request_timeout: 10
  fallbacks: [{"zephyr-beta": ["gpt-5.6-luna"]}]
  allowed_fails: 3

quote: This method can reduce the number of failed retrievals by 49% and, when combined with reranking, by 67%.
author: Anthropic

claim: Breakdown: contextual embeddings alone 35%, plus contextual BM25 49%
quote: Contextual Embeddings reduced the top-20-chunk retrieval failure rate by 35% (5.7% → 3.7%). Combining Contextual Embeddings and Contextual BM25 reduced the top-20-chunk retrieval failure rate by 49% (5.7% → 2.9%).
author: Anthropic
note: With reranking: 5.7% to 1.9% (67%), per WebFetch summary of the same page.

claim: Chunk context is short and prepended before embedding and BM25 indexing
quote: The resulting contextual text, usually 50-100 tokens, is prepended to the chunk before embedding it and before creating the BM25 index.
author: Anthropic

claim: One-time cost of contextualising with prompt caching
quote: the one-time cost to generate contextualized chunks is $1.02 per million document tokens
author: Anthropic
note: Assumes 800-token chunks, 8k-token documents, 50 token instructions, 100 tokens of context per chunk.

claim: Metric used: 1 minus recall@20 over top-20 chunks
quote: We use 1 minus recall@20 as our evaluation metric, which measures the percentage of relevant documents that fail to be retrieved within the top 20 chunks.
author: Anthropic
note: Sentence end ('top 20 chunks') completed from context; verify if quoted in full.

quote: An HNSW index creates a multilayer graph. It has better query performance than IVFFlat (in terms of speed-recall tradeoff), but has slower build times and uses more memory.
author: pgvector (Andrew Kane)

quote: An IVFFlat index divides vectors into lists, and then searches a subset of those lists that are closest to the query vector. It has faster build times and uses less memory than HNSW, but has lower query performance (in terms of speed-recall tradeoff).
author: pgvector (Andrew Kane)

quote: Indexes build significantly faster when the graph fits into `maintenance_work_mem`
author: pgvector (Andrew Kane)
note: HNSW can be created on an empty table (no training step), unlike IVFFlat.

claim: IVFFlat build: after data, lists sizing
quote: Create the index *after* the table has some data ... a good place to start is `rows / 1000` for up to 1M rows and `sqrt(rows)` for over 1M rows
author: pgvector (Andrew Kane)
note: Two items of a numbered list joined with '...'. Indexable vector type: up to 2,000 dimensions.

quote: Starting search from the upper layer together with utilizing the scale separation boosts the performance compared to NSW and allows a logarithmic complexity scaling.
author: Yu. A. Malkov, D. A. Yashunin

quote: 1536 for text-embedding-3-small or 3072 for text-embedding-3-large
author: OpenAI docs
note: Max input 8192 tokens; dimensions parameter can shorten embeddings. 1536 floats x 4 bytes = 6 KB per vector (our arithmetic).

author: OpenAI docs
note: Per 1M input tokens, from the model page via WebFetch. Guide lists 62,500 pages per dollar for 3-small (about 800 tokens per page), consistent with $0.02/1M. Prices change; date-stamp on page.

claim: LinkedIn KG-RAG over historical support tickets
quote: constructs a KG from historical issues for use in retrieval, retaining the intra-issue structure and inter-issue relations
author: Zhentao Xu, Mark Jerome Cruz, Matthew Guevara, Tie Wang, Manasi Deshpande, Xiaofeng Wang, Zheng Li (LinkedIn)
note: Quote from abstract via WebFetch; wording may begin 'Our method constructs'.

claim: LinkedIn KG-RAG retrieval and production result
quote: our method outperforms the baseline by 77.6% in MRR and by 0.32 in BLEU ... reduced the median per-issue resolution time by 28.6%
author: Zhentao Xu, Mark Jerome Cruz, Matthew Guevara, Tie Wang, Manasi Deshpande, Xiaofeng Wang, Zheng Li (LinkedIn)
note: Two abstract fragments joined with '...'; the 28.6% is after deployment in LinkedIn's customer service team for about six months (per abstract, verify wording).

claim: DoorDash RAG flow: condense conversation, retrieve similar resolved cases and KB articles
quote: Because the issue likely will be spread across several messages and follow-up questions, the system first condenses the entire conversation to pinpoint the core problem. Using this summary, it then searches historical data for the top N similar cases previously resolved with information from KB articles.
author: Zhe Jia, Shuai Wang, Aditi Bamba, Martin Wang (DoorDash)
note: Fetched via Wayback snapshot 2026-07-13; original doordash.engineering post likely mid-2024 (unconfirmed).

claim: DoorDash three components: RAG, LLM Guardrail, LLM Judge
quote: we developed three systems to resolve the RAG challenges: LLM Guardrail, LLM Judge, and a quality improvement pipeline
author: Zhe Jia, Shuai Wang, Aditi Bamba, Martin Wang (DoorDash)

quote: This guardrail system has successfully reduced overall hallucinations by 90% and cut down potentially severe compliance issues by 99%.
author: Zhe Jia, Shuai Wang, Aditi Bamba, Martin Wang (DoorDash)

quote: Generally speaking, larger prompts lead to slower responses.
author: Zhe Jia, Shuai Wang, Aditi Bamba, Martin Wang (DoorDash)
note: Preceded by: latency can vary from a sub-second level to tens of seconds.

quote: increasing the percentage of acceptable answers by a relative 27% and reducing incorrect advice by a relative 60% through our transition from a traditional RAG architecture to an enhanced agentic RAG approach
author: Arnab Chakraborty, Christopher Settles, Adi Raghavendra (Uber)

claim: Uber EAg-RAG hybrid retrieval with enriched metadata
quote: we introduced an additional BM25-based retriever alongside traditional vector search. This retriever fetches the most relevant document chunks using enriched metadata, which includes summaries, FAQs, and keywords for each chunk.
author: Arnab Chakraborty, Christopher Settles, Adi Raghavendra (Uber)
note: Corpus: 40+ security and privacy policy documents; golden set of 100+ SME test queries; Genie is Uber's Slack on-call copilot.

quote: ATF is deployed and currently serving 9,000 async tasks scheduled per second and in use by 28 engineering teams internally
author: Arun Sai Krishnan (Dropbox)

quote: It currently supports 100+ use cases which require either immediate or delayed task scheduling.
author: Arun Sai Krishnan (Dropbox)

quote: Lambda: A callback implementing business logic. Task: Unit of execution of a lambda.
author: Arun Sai Krishnan (Dropbox)

quote: The ATF system guarantees that a task is executed at least once after being scheduled. Execution is said to be complete once the user-defined callback signals task completion to the ATF system.
author: Arun Sai Krishnan (Dropbox)

quote: The ATF system guarantees that at most one instance of a task will be actively executing at any given in point.
author: Arun Sai Krishnan (Dropbox)
note: Typo 'given in point' is in the original.

quote: 95% of tasks begin execution within five seconds from their scheduled execution time.
author: Arun Sai Krishnan (Dropbox)

claim: ATF Store Consumer polls the task store
quote: The Store Consumer is a service that periodically polls the task store to find tasks that are ready for execution and pushes them onto the right queues
author: Arun Sai Krishnan (Dropbox)
note: Components: Frontend (RPC), Task Store (Edgestore), Store Consumer, Queue (SQS), Controller, Executor, Heartbeat and Status Controller (HSC).

claim: ATF queue is SQS as buffer
quote: ATF uses AWS Simple Queue Service (SQS) to queue tasks internally. These queues act as a buffer between the Store Consumer and Controllers
author: Arun Sai Krishnan (Dropbox)

quote: While processing, Executor performs Heartbeat RPC calls to Heartbeat and Status Controller (HSC). Once processing is done, Executor performs TaskStatus RPC call to HSC
author: Arun Sai Krishnan (Dropbox)

claim: Google Cron: prefer skipping to double launching
quote: The approach we will be leaning towards in this article is to prefer skipping launches, instead of risking double launches, as much as the infrastructure allows.
author: Štěpán Davidovič, Kavita Guliani (Google)
note: Fetched via Wayback snapshot.

quote: undoing a double launch may be difficult, and in some cases (consider the newsletter example) impossible. So, we prefer to "fail closed" (in engineering terminology) to avoid systemically creating bad state.
author: Štěpán Davidovič, Kavita Guliani (Google)

claim: Google Cron: idempotent vs non-idempotent jobs
quote: Some Cron jobs are idempotent, and in case of system malfunction, it is safe to launch them multiple times [dash] for example, garbage collection. Other Cron jobs should not be launched twice, for example, a process that sends out an email newsletter
author: Štěpán Davidovič, Kavita Guliani (Google)
note: The original has an em-dash where [dash] stands; replace with a colon or parentheses on the page (repo rule).

quote: it is more acceptable to not launch Cron jobs for a while than to mistakenly launch the same Cron job ten times instead of once.
author: Štěpán Davidovič, Kavita Guliani (Google)

quote: We deploy multiple replicas of the Cron service and use the Paxos algorithm to ensure consistent state among them.
author: Štěpán Davidovič, Kavita Guliani (Google)
note: SRE book wording: 'use the Paxos distributed consensus algorithm'. Only the leader replica launches jobs.

claim: Google Cron: launch synchronisation points and idempotent external ops
quote: all operations on external systems, which we may need to continue upon re-election, either have to be idempotent (i.e., we can safely do them again), or we need to be able to look up their state and see whether they completed or not, unambiguously.
author: Štěpán Davidovič, Kavita Guliani (Google)
note: Preceded by: every launch has two synchronization points, when about to launch and when finished.

claim: SRE book chapter 24 wording of the trade-off
quote: In general, we favor skipping launches rather than risking double launches, as much as the infrastructure allows.
author: Štěpán Davidovič; edited by Kavita Guliani (Google)

quote: On our busiest days, the system processes over 1.4 billion jobs at a peak rate of 33,000 per second.
author: Saroj Yadav, Matthew Smillie, Mike Demmer, Tyler Johnson (Slack)
note: Date shown on page is December 6, 2017 with 'Updated: June 25, 2020'; the post is commonly cited as 2020, so the 2017 date may be a migration artifact (unconfirmed).

claim: Slack failure: Redis hit its memory limit and could not enqueue
quote: Resource contention in our database layer led to a slowdown in the execution of jobs, which caused Redis to reach its maximum configured memory limit. At this point, because Redis had no free memory, we could no longer enqueue new jobs
author: Saroj Yadav, Matthew Smillie, Mike Demmer, Tyler Johnson (Slack)

claim: Slack: Kafka in front of Redis as minimum viable change
quote: In the spirit of pursuing a minimum viable change, we decided to add Kafka in front of Redis rather than replacing Redis with Kafka outright.
author: Saroj Yadav, Matthew Smillie, Mike Demmer, Tyler Johnson (Slack)

quote: we developed Kafkagate, a new stateless service written in Go, to enqueue jobs to Kafka. Kafkagate exposes a simple HTTP POST interface whereby each request contains a Kafka topic, partition, and content.
author: Saroj Yadav, Matthew Smillie, Mike Demmer, Tyler Johnson (Slack)

quote: JQRelay is a stateless service written in Go that relays jobs from a Kafka topic to its corresponding Redis cluster.
author: Saroj Yadav, Matthew Smillie, Mike Demmer, Tyler Johnson (Slack)
note: Verbatim from WebFetch extract; not re-checked in local text.

quote: Maestro now launches thousands of workflow instances and runs half a million jobs daily on average, and has completed around 2 million jobs on particularly busy days.
author: Jun He, Natallia Dzenisenka, Praneeth Yenugutala, Yingyi Zhang, Anjali Norwood (Netflix)
note: Open-sourced in this post. 'Maestro is a horizontally scalable workflow orchestrator designed to manage large-scale Data/ML workflows'. Fetched via Wayback.

claim: Netflix RENO hybrid push and pull
quote: We therefore chose a hybrid Push AND Pull communication model wherein the server tries to deliver notifications to all devices immediately using Push notifications, and devices call home at various stages of the application lifecycle.
author: Ankush Gulati, David Gevorkyan (Netflix)
note: Fetched via Wayback.

quote: At peak times, RENO serves about 150k events per second.
author: Ankush Gulati, David Gevorkyan (Netflix)

quote: We thus assigned a priority to each use case and sharded event traffic by routing to priority-specific queues and the corresponding event processing clusters.
author: Ankush Gulati, David Gevorkyan (Netflix)
note: Queues are Amazon SQS; persistent store is Cassandra so devices can poll; push via Zuul Push.
